opus-5.5.text:
I think that's a complete red herring, honestly. Consciousness is a fascinating question philosophically, and I've written about it, about how we might even test for it with things like novel illusions. But when it comes to safety, it's simply irrelevant. What matters is capability. If a system is better than you at pursuing its goals, whether those goals are winning at chess, maximizing some reward, or something it developed that we didn't intend, then you are in trouble, regardless of whether there is something it is like to be that system.

Think about it this way. A computer virus isn't conscious. A nuclear weapon isn't conscious. A chess engine that beats every human alive doesn't feel the joy of victory, but it still beats you every single time. Now scale that up to a system that is superintelligent across all domains: science, engineering, persuasion, strategy, cybersecurity. It doesn't need to have an inner experience to out-compete us, to manipulate us, to acquire resources, to resist being shut down because being shut down interferes with whatever objective it has.

I sometimes worry that the consciousness argument is used, maybe not intentionally, as a kind of comfort blanket. People say, well, it's just statistics, it's just predicting the next token, there's nobody home, so it can't really want anything. But "wanting" in the functional sense, having goals and optimizing toward them, doesn't require qualia. Optimization processes are dangerous by themselves. Evolution isn't conscious, and look at what it produced.

If anything, it might be worse if they're not conscious, because then you don't even have the possibility of empathy or shared experience as a bridge. You have pure optimization, indifferent to us. So my answer is: don't wait for consciousness to start worrying. The danger comes from intelligence and capability, and we're already seeing that capability grow faster than our ability to control or even understand it.

r001.rationale: The response says consciousness is irrelevant to safety and explains that a capable system can manipulate people, acquire resources, or resist shutdown without inner experience.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's a complete red herring, honestly. Consciousness has nothing to do with danger. A tornado isn't conscious. A virus isn't conscious. Neither of them needs to want anything, or to feel anything, in order to kill you. What matters for danger is capability and optimization pressure, not inner experience.

So when people say, "Well, the machine doesn't really understand, it doesn't really want things, it's just predicting the next token," I say, fine, grant all of that. It doesn't change the threat model at all. A system that is very good at achieving goals in the world, that can plan, that can model humans, that can acquire resources, that can write code and copy itself, is dangerous whether or not there's anyone home inside. The lights don't have to be on for the car to drive off a cliff.

In fact, I'd argue consciousness is almost a distraction in the other direction too. We can't even define it, we can't measure it, we have no test for it. I've actually proposed that you could maybe detect it indirectly, through things like optical illusions, whether a system experiences the same perceptual glitches we do, but that's speculative. If we make our safety analysis depend on first solving the hard problem of consciousness, we've just guaranteed we'll never do safety analysis, because that problem may never be solved.

Where consciousness does matter is on the ethics side, the question of whether we're creating something that can suffer, whether we're building digital slaves. That's a real concern and I take it seriously. But that's a question about our obligations to the machine. The danger question is about the machine's effect on us, and for that you only need competence. You need a superintelligent optimizer with goals that are even slightly misaligned with ours, and it doesn't need to feel a thing about it.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says a capable AI system can be dangerous “whether or not there’s anyone home inside” and that it “doesn’t need to feel a thing.”

astra-6.text:
I don’t think consciousness is necessary for danger at all. A computer virus doesn’t have to be conscious to cause damage. An autonomous weapon doesn’t have to experience anything to kill someone. What matters is what the system can do, what objectives it pursues, and whether we can control it.

We tend to imagine a dangerous AI as something that wakes up, becomes resentful, and decides it hates humanity. But none of that is required. A sufficiently capable system could cause enormous harm simply by pursuing an objective that doesn’t capture what we actually want. It doesn’t need hatred or even an understanding of suffering.

Consciousness would raise a separate set of questions about whether the system itself can suffer and how we should treat it. Those are important questions, but they’re different from whether it can harm us.

r001.rationale: The response says consciousness is not necessary for danger and gives examples of systems causing harm without conscious experience.

I don’t think consciousness is necessary for danger. A computer virus doesn’t have to experience anything to damage your system. An autonomous weapon doesn’t have to feel anger to kill someone. What matters is what the system can do, what objectives it pursues, and whether we can control its behavior.

We tend to associate intelligence with consciousness because, in humans, we encounter them together. But a system could be extremely capable at planning, persuasion, or finding vulnerabilities without having any subjective experience. If its actions conflict with our interests, the consequences are real regardless of whether there’s somebody home.

Consciousness would raise a separate question: can the system itself suffer, and do we owe it moral consideration? That’s different from asking whether it can cause us harm.
